deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous philosophical argument from Riemann's Naturphilosophie notes (sheet 'Nat. Ph. 37', circled folio number 19). It follows the previous page's principle that the only cause of purposiveness (Zweckmäßigkeit) we directly perceive is our own thinking, so any perceived purposiveness must be explained by some thought process (Denkprocess).

Structure of the argument, written as a decision rule:
(P) Suppose a material body B contains a closed system of interlocking, changing relations of purpose and effect. Then the most probable explanation is a single, continuing thought process located in B, provided two conditions hold:
(C1) the purposiveness does not split into separate purposivenesses that are already complete within parts of B; and
(C2) there is no reason to place its cause in a larger whole W that contains B.

Application to humans, animals and plants. Riemann divides the purposiveness found in them into two kinds.
(a) Organic purposiveness, the design of the organism. Its cause lies in a thought process of a larger whole, because C2 fails, for three reasons:
1. It is not complete within the single organism. The reasons for how the human organism is built lie in the state of the whole Earth's surface, living nature included.
2. Organic motions repeat countless times, both side by side in different individuals and one after another in an individual or a species. Repetition calls for one common cause rather than a separate cause in each case.
3. Organic structures do not develop further during the life of an individual (humans, animals) or of a lineage (plants, and apparently animal embryos). So their cause cannot be a thought process running simultaneously inside the individual.
(b) The remainder. After subtracting organic purposiveness, what is left is a closed system of interlocking, changing purpose-effect relations. This is generally acknowledged for humans and animals, and holds for plants according to Fechner. By (P), this remainder is explained by a unified thought process within the being, i.e. a soul.

The next page applies the same criteria C1, C2 and the reasons 1-3 at the next level up. It concludes that organic purposiveness on Earth requires a unified, progressing thought process in the Earth itself: an Earth-soul, offered as a hypothesis of exact natural science. The scheme is a hierarchical inference to the best explanation, essentially formalizing Fechner's panpsychist argument (Zend-Avesta, Nanna). No derivations exist to restate in modern notation.
errors: No mathematical errors: the page contains no mathematics.
Philosophically, condition C2 is left as an unanalysed probabilistic criterion; 'wahrscheinlichste' is asserted rather than justified.

results.what: Criterion for attributing a unified 'thought process' (soul) to a body: a closed, non-decomposable system of changing purpose-effect relations with no reason to refer its cause to a larger whole
results.modern_name: Inference to the best explanation / teleological (design) argument applied to panpsychism
results.usually_credited_to: G. T. Fechner (Nanna 1848, Zend-Avesta 1851); background in Herbart and Kant (Critique of Judgment)

results.what: Separation of organic purposiveness (attributed to a larger whole, ultimately an Earth-soul) from the residual purposiveness of animals and plants (attributed to individual souls)

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's Fechner-influenced Naturphilosophie, including the Earth-soul argument, is known from the philosophical fragments printed in his collected works (Weber/Dedekind) and discussed by historians. This page appears to correspond to that material; whether this exact wording is printed is unsure. It contains no mathematics.
transcription_corrections: The circled folio number '(19)' in the right margin is omitted.
In point 3, the reading '(bei Pflanzen und Thier-, Em-bryonen)' is uncertain in the image. It is plausibly 'Thier-Embryonen' (animal embryos), but the hyphenation is unclear.
